evidence.text: 人相違也。从大凵聲。凡去之屬皆从去。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 大 (“man”) + 口 (“mouth, object”). Top figure simplified to 土, unrelated to 士 (“scholar, gentleman”), while bottom simplified to 厶; a conservative variant is 厺.
There are various interpretations of the combination of “man” and “mouth, object”. One is that the ideograph represented a man with a hole marked in his crotch, with the idea of “anus” (i.e. getting rid of) (Schuessler, 2007). Another is that it represented a man departing from a cave or city.
Alternatively, it may be the original character of 呿 (OC *kʰal, *kʰas, *kʰab, “to open one's mouth”), the meaning given by the combination of 大 (“big”) and 口 (“mouth”). The meaning “to depart” would be an extension of the meaning “to open one's mouth”, as the lips depart from each other when one's mouth is open.
Shuowen Jiezi interprets the character as a phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *kʰaʔ, *kʰas): semantic 大 (“man”) + phonetic 𠙴 (qū).
In addition, 去 is also the original character of 盍 (OC *ɡaːb, “to cover”). The 大 could be a cover on top of an object 口.
The man on top is simplified as 土 as in 赤 and 走 (< 𧺆).
There were two pronunciations in Middle Chinese. The rising tone pronunciation originally meant “to put away, to eliminate” (causative of “to go away”), and the falling tone “to go away, to leave, to depart” (anticausative). The merger of the two pronunciations already happened in Old Chinese and most extant dialects do not observe this distinction now.
This word is of Sino-Tibetan origin with the basic meaning of "to get rid of". Compare Tibetan སྐྱག (skyag, “to spend, to lay out; dung, excrement”), རྐྱག (rkyag, “dirt, excrement”), Burmese ကျ (kya., “to fall, to become low”), ချ (hkya., “to put down, to bring down, to lower”).

evidence.text: The entry lists oracle-bone evidence in 合集 7473, bronze evidence in 集成 02782, Chu manuscripts, and the Shuowen small-seal form. Its account reads the upper shape as a person and the lower as a cave opening, with the lower element simplified to 凵 in small seal. This is a sourced interpretation of the graph, not settled fact: a Fudan paleographic article disputes the usual oracle-bone reading.
evidence.title: 漢字「去」：字形演變

evidence.source: Fudan University Center for the Study of Excavated Texts and Paleography; Yang Huaiyuan and Sun Yingqiong
evidence.field: sections 1, 3, 4; oracle-bone forms and meaning history
evidence.text: The authors review competing analyses of oracle-bone 去: one proposal reads a 大+口 form as the precursor of 呿, ‘open the mouth,’ and distinguishes a vessel-with-cover graph as 盍; their own analysis instead identifies oracle-bone 去 as the early form of 盍. They argue that the departure sense later differentiated from 盍, and that Shuowen’s analysis ‘从大凵聲’ misidentifies the graph’s elements. They report that departure is not securely established in oracle-bone inscriptions; earlier proposed readings of two inscriptions as ‘leave’ or ‘go to’ are challenged. Their proposed semantic link—removing a cover as a reversal of covering—is an analysis, not a directly documented transition.

evidence.source: Fudan University Center for the Study of Excavated Texts and Paleography; Yang Huaiyuan and Sun Yingqiong
evidence.text: The authors cite departure-sense examples in the received Zhouyi and Shijing, including 《詩經·大雅·生民》‘鳥乃去矣’ and 《小雅·斯干》‘鳥鼠攸去’. They characterize these as Western Zhou uses, while noting the texts are transmitted works; this does not supply an independently dated manuscript occurrence. They also warn that 《尚書·胤征》 is from the ‘Old Text Shangshu’, considered a later fabrication, and should not be used as early evidence.
evidence.title: 釋甲骨文中的“去”——兼論上古“去”聲字的韻尾

evidence.source: Fudan University Center for the Study of Excavated Texts and Paleography; Yang Huaiyuan and Sun Yingqiong
evidence.text: The article reports an earlier proposal that the oracle graph from 大 and 口 means opening the mouth and is the source of 呿, and a competing vessel-cover analysis associated with 盍. It rejects the former as unsupported by its account of oracle-bone composition and advances the latter. It separately describes departure 去 as differentiated from 盍 rather than a straightforward graphic loan. It also surveys disagreement in the Old Chinese rhyme classification of 去-series words. The excerpt does not independently establish the original pronunciation or depicted referent of the vessel graph, nor does it establish an early attestation of the word 呿 as the source of the departure word.

gaps: The sources disagree on whether the earliest 去 graph depicts a person leaving an opening, an open mouth (related to 呿), or a covered vessel (identified by one study as 盍). No glyph image was visually inspected in this research pass; graph identities and shapes are reported from the sources' descriptions and catalogue references.

The Fudan article argues the departure word differentiated from 盍, but the proposed cover-removal semantic bridge is an author analysis, not a documented chain of dated attestations. Secure departure meaning is not established in the oracle-bone examples discussed; the article cites received Zhouyi and Shijing passages as early literary evidence, without providing manuscript dating for those exact passages.

A sound-based borrowing of the departure word from 呿 remains unproven here. The early name/pronunciation of any depicted mouth or vessel is not independently recovered, and no dated early 呿 attestation was verified. Do not treat 呿 as established original sound/source of 去.

Shuowen’s Han-dynasty explanation 人相違也。从大凵聲 is recorded in the dossier but was not independently opened in this pass. The Fudan study explicitly contests its component analysis; the Academia Sinica database presents the cave-exit interpretation.

The local kMandarin and Baxter–Sagart rows were checked from supplied inputs. Exact upstream per-character Unihan pages were attempted but inaccessible in the browser.
